headlines.title: Couple charged with murder in deadly shooting of son-in-law at Dublin park
headlines.description: Prosecutors have filed charges against an elderly couple accused of fatally shooting their son-in-law at the Dublin Sports Grounds over the weekend. The Alameda County District Attorney’s Office charged 77-year-old couple Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen with murder and other charges in the shooting of their son-in-law, 40-year-old Jonathan McKinsey. The couple had yet to appear before a judge at the East County Hall of Justice as of Wednesday morning. Court records indicate McKinsey was in the middle of a contentious divorce and custody battle with his wife. McKinsey claimed in court filings that his wife had a history of physically assaulting him and had allowed her parents to abuse him as well. Dublin Sep 27 Dublin Sep 29 McKinsey, who was a transgender man, also alleged that his father-in-law punched him in the chest after he underwent a double mastectomy in 2010. He also claimed his mother-in-law called him a “disgusting queer” and a pervert. McKinsey’s divorce attorney, Andrea Mah, called the loss of her client a “true tragedy.” “I trust that our justice system will hold those responsible for Mr. McKinsey’s senseless death accountable,” Mah said in a statement. Court records also show McKinsey, an tech executive at The New York Times, pleaded not guilty last year to misdemeanor child abuse charges linked to accusations that he slapped one of his children and left another young child alone while he went shopping. In restraining order documents, McKinsey’s estranged wife alleged that she and her children endured years of physical, verbal and emotional abuse by McKinsey. In his own request for a restraining order, McKinsey wrote, “I am desperately afraid of what Candice will do to take revenge on me.”

headlines.title: Delivery impersonators arrested for alleged home invasion attempt in San Jose
headlines.description: Two young men from Texas were arrested on suspicion of trying to break into a San Jose home while pretending to be delivery service workers, police said Wednesday. The alleged home invasion attempt occurred on Sept. 5 in South San Jose, police said. Two people – one wearing a delivery service outfit and the other a ski mask – were seen in surveillance footage trying to deliver a package to the 911 caller’s residence when the person wearing the ski mask pulled out a gun. The two people fled from the home in a vehicle before officers arrived. Detectives used automated license plate reader data to identify the suspects’ vehicle and later the suspects as Dallas residents Damian Vielma, 20, and Jeremiah Clybourn, 19. During their investigation, detectives uncovered evidence linking Vielma and Clybourn to multiple crimes across various jurisdictions, including Atherton, police said. Vielma and Clybourn tended to target victims with high amounts of crypto wealth while posing as delivery personnel. Vielma and Clybourn were arrested in Dallas last Thursday, police said. Authorities found evidence of the alleged crime and various guns while serving a search warrant. Vielma and Clybourn were booked into jail for multiple crimes, including attempted robbery, vehicle theft and firearm-related crimes, according to police. They are awaiting extradition back to the Bay Area. Anyone with information about this case or similar cases is encouraged to contact San Jose police Detective Ledesma by email at 4842@sanjoseca.gov or by phone at 408-277-4166.

headlines.title: Proposition to allow cars back on the Great Highway heads to San Francisco voters
headlines.description: For the second time, San Francisco voters will get to have a say on the contentious battle over the Great Highway as some westside residents are fighting to reopen the closed road to cars on weekdays. If passed in November, Prop G would reopen the road to cars Monday through Friday and keep it as a park on the weekends — which supporters call the “compromise.” The compromise was in effect during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown when fewer cars were on the road and people were looking for outdoor spaces to enjoy. The measure seeks to reverse Proposition K, a November 2024 ballot measure that fully shut the 2-mile stretch of road to cars and turned the site into a coastal park along Ocean Beach, now called Sunset Dunes. “At the end of the day, I prioritize those that need to commute to work or school on weekdays over weekday recreational needs for the road,” said Supervisor Alan Wong, a Prop G supporter, in an interview. Wong represents District 4, which encompasses the Sunset district, where the Upper Great Highway is located. Prop K officially closed the Upper Great Highway to cars on March 14, 2025. Streetlights at intersections were removed, and park structures and amenities began popping up. The group on the other side of the issue that’s been advocating to keep the road as a full-time park is called “Friends of Sunset Dunes.” “This park and this space is evolving,” said the group’s President Lucas Lux in an interview. “We’re putting out for folks what we have heard they want, places for their children to play, places to learn and to be in nature.” After the road shut down, a group of voters and residents on San Francisco’s west side, where a majority voted against Prop K, started a movement to reopen the Great Highway back to cars and return to the “compromise.” The group, called “Great Highway for Everyone,” received enough signatures to qualify its measure for the upcoming November election. “I think that it’s fair to allow sharing of the road for vehicle access on weekdays when there’s a high demand for commuter access during those times,” Wong said. Prop G supporters argue that traffic injuries in the Sunset district have gone up since the closure since traffic that once relied on the Great Highway is being diverted to other nearby roads. “Since the Great Highway closed, traffic injuries in Sunset neighborhoods have risen sharply — a serious an unacceptable threat to public safety,” wrote Richard Corriea in an official Prop G proponent argument submitted to the Department of Elections. Corriea leads the “Yes on G” campaign. However, the data tells a different story. In all of 2024, there were 106 traffic collisions resulting in injury in District 4, compared to 99 in all of 2025, according to data from the San Francisco Police Department and the Department of Public Health. Friends of Sunset Dunes and other pedestrian safety advocate groups have called out the Yes on G campaign for its claims on traffic crashes in the Sunset. “The data is very clear that crashes are actually down in the neighborhood,” Lux said. “It’s fair to have a preference of wanting this to be a road, but let’s not resort to lying to voters to get that.” Some roads near the park did see an increase in traffic congestion in the months following the closure, according to a study from the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency. Those roads include the Lower Great Highway and Chain of Lakes Drive. Muni buses experienced minor increases in travel times on 19th Avenue. Friends of Sunset Dunes and others against Prop G say that the measure will “destroy” the park, including a new children’s playground that opened over the weekend on the roadway. “If Prop G passes, the playground has to go, the skate park has to go, every park feature has to go,” Lux said. The City Controller’s Office says that making the road suitable for cars would “significantly increase the cost of government,” wrote Deputy Controller ChiaYu Ma in a letter to the city’s Department of Elections. Adding in new traffic signals, restriping the road, erecting signage, and removing park amenities could cost the city about $10 million, the Controller’s Office says. Additional annual expenses for sand removal could cost anywhere from $100,000 to $1.5 million annually. But the city could also save around $300,000 per year since it won’t need to hire full-time staff to maintain the park, the Controller’s Office estimates. Those against Prop G also say that closing the park on the weekdays will have an additional social cost, with the consequence of fewer recreational opportunities. Supervisor Myrna Melgar, a staunch opponent of Prop G, pointed to the dozens of children having fun on the new pirate-themed playground which opened Saturday. Melgar said in an interview that Prop G “takes away the value for these little guys because they’re going to grow up with this park.” One year after the park’s opening, the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department analyzed visitor statistics. It found that the park averages 3,800 visitors on weekdays and 7,200 visitors on weekend days. But Wong says that there are plenty of recreational spaces already in the area, like Golden Gate Park, Ocean Beach, Lake Merced and Stern Grove Park. “I think that with the available recreational spaces, it’s a fair compromise to allow use of the roadway for commuter travel during weekdays,” he said. Registered voters in San Francisco can expect their official ballot packets to arrive in the mail in early October. Residents can check their voter registration status at sfelections.org. Voter pamphlets have already started arriving in the mail, which are packets that include a sample ballot, information about local candidates and ballot measures, an explanation of ranked-choice voting, and instructions for voting by mail or in person.

headlines.title: San Jose City Council approves municipal garage rate hikes, puts street parking meter increases on hold
headlines.description: Parking in downtown San Jose is about to get more expensive, though not quite as pricey as city leaders originally proposed. The City Council voted Tuesday night to approve higher rates at several municipal garages while putting a controversial plan to raise street parking rates on hold. The garage behind San Pedro Square is among those where drivers will soon pay more. Under the new plan, motorists will still get their first 90 minutes free, but the hourly rate after that will increase by $1. In addition, special event parking rates will rise by $5. The decision follows more than two hours of public comment and debate as downtown businesses continue working to bring customers back. “I just don’t see why I should continue to invest in the city that won’t invest in me,” said Cache Bouren, a local bar owner who opposed the broader rate hikes. Councilmember Anthony Tordillos of District 3, who represents downtown, acknowledged the delicate balance facing local merchants. “I think the big concerns are still about the fact that downtown is still in recovery post-pandemic,” Tordillos said. The council ultimately rejected two other major proposals: raising street meter rates from their current levels and extending meter enforcement until 9 p.m. However, those proposals could return as the city looks for ways to pay for parking garage maintenance and equipment upgrades. “Staff is going to do more analysis to figure out what are the revenue needs to maintain our garages, do equipment upgrades for things like our meters—we need to see how we replenish those funds and make it sustainable,” Tordillos explained. For some residents, the shifting costs are already altering how they visit the city core. “I feel like either way, you’re going to have to pay. There’s no more free parking. You get lucky if you get free parking,” said Ana, a San Jose resident. “It’s always, ‘I have to pay, so let’s just Uber.’ At the end of the day, it’s cheaper.” The council also voted to expand a discounted parking program for eligible downtown employees. As for the street meter increases, they are off the table for now, but city staff will continue studying how to cover the cost of maintaining San Jose’s parking system.

headlines.title: HUD's $4B grant program aims to reduce homelessness, but will it do the opposite?
headlines.description: The federal government is drastically changing the way homeless programs throughout America are funded, but nonprofits and local governments warn the move could put roughly 100,000 people at risk of losing their housing. “This is a population that, by definition, needs stability,” said Tony LoPresti, the top attorney for Santa Clara County, which joined other local governments and nonprofits across the country in filing suit against the federal government seeking to have the new funding restrictions thrown out. “These are new rules that go against decades of evidence that have proven what works when it comes to homelessness prevention.” Tony LoPresti is Santa Clara County’s lead attorney, who is overseeing the county’s lawsuit against HUD that was filed in an effort to block new restrictions on federal funding meant to combat homelessness. New HUD rules favor temporary housing for homeless over long-term programs At issue are major policy changes being implemented by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, which aim to steer federal funding away from homeless programs that offer long-term subsidized housing and instead prioritize initiatives that provide transitional or temporary housing. For communities across the U.S., including in the Bay Area, the changes could result in millions of dollars in funding cuts to individual homelessness programs. “It’s hard to overstate how important this battle is,” LoPresti said. “You’re going to have local governments and other service providers that are going have to make a deeply problematic choice about whether they’re going pull from other pots of funding to sustain a program or cut the program altogether.” HUD’s grant process, known as the Continuum of Care (CoC) Program Competition, is making more than $4 billion available for homelessness programs as part of its 2026 application process. While permanent housing programs have historically received about 90 percent of the funding, HUD is now setting aside $1.3 billion, or about a third of the funding, for new projects prioritizing transitional housing as well as supportive services that don’t include housing, like job training and substance use treatment programs. HUD is also prioritizing housing programs that require participants to engage in certain services, such as job training and substance use treatment, as a condition of receiving federally subsidized housing. Federal govt. is reshaping homelessness policies in a significant way The change represents a major shift in U.S. homelessness policy. Beginning with the George W. Bush administration in the early 2000s, the federal government increasingly embraced what became known as a Housing First approach, which focuses on placing people experiencing homelessness into permanent housing without requiring preconditions, such as rehab or mental health services. “I’m worried for myself and I’m also worried there’s going to be more and more people homeless,” said Daniel Hayward, who lives at a federally subsidized housing facility in Oakland that is now at risk of losing funding because of HUD’s new policies. “It’s frustrating – the anxiety, that pressure, it just builds on you.” Hayward spent three years homeless, living in the backseat of his small car, prior to moving into the permanent housing facility, which now provides shelter and supportive services to Hayward and roughly 100 other people. “If you don’t have the permanent housing, you’re just going to move people from one place to another,” Hayward said. “It’s temporary – that’s the whole word, temporary. We need the permanent solution.” Daniel Hayward, who become homeless at 60 years old, is once again in danger of losing his housing in light of HUD’s new funding restrictions that steer money away from long-term housing subsidies, like the one currently funding Hayward’s 100-person apartment building in Oakland. While researchers and homeless advocates have long viewed the Housing First model as a best practice, the Trump administration has characterized it as a “failure,” repeatedly pointing to increased government spending and a rise in homelessness over the past decade. HUD counted 745,652 people experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2025. Housing alone will not solve a crisis driven by addiction and mental illness. Under President Trump’s leadership, HUD is making necessary reforms to put recovery first. Scott Turner, HUD Secretary “The ‘housing first’ experiment failed Americans by warehousing the vulnerable without results,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner noted in an agency press release back in June announcing the start of this year’s grant process. “Housing alone will not solve a crisis driven by addiction and mental illness. Under President Trump’s leadership, HUD is making necessary reforms to put recovery first.” HUD Secretary Scott Turner has voiced sharp criticism for the federal government’s long-held homeless policy known as Housing First, which prioritizes providing long-term housing to the homeless without requiring preconditions such as rehab or job training. “The ‘housing first’ experiment failed Americans by warehousing the vulnerable without results,” Turner said. HUD’s new funding policies run counter to its own previous research HUD says its approach is intended to address what it describes as the underlying causes of homelessness by directing more funding toward treatment, recovery, job training, and other services designed to promote self-sufficiency. HUD’s criticism of the Housing First model, however, differs sharply from its own previous findings. “The research literature has nearly reached consensus that providing permanent housing—without mandating sobriety, treatment, or service participation to demonstrate housing readiness—is effective in helping people exit homelessness and achieve long-term housing stability,” HUD noted in a 2024 report. In response to the apparent contradiction, a HUD spokesperson told NBC Bay Area “Housing First has failed our most vulnerable and enabled addiction,” adding “the data proves it, and it is shameful the Biden administration doubled down on this failed policy.” Homeless advocates and service providers say temporary housing, including transitional housing facilities, provides a necessary service for people experiencing homelessness, but argue shifting funding away from permanent housing in order to provide more temporary beds will only hurt an already vulnerable population. There’s absolutely nothing wrong with temporary solutions, but absent permanent solutions, they don’t go anywhere. Vivian Wan, CEO of Abode Services “There’s absolutely nothing wrong with temporary solutions, but absent permanent solutions, they don’t go anywhere,” said Vivian Wan, CEO of Abode Services, a nonprofit that provides housing and homelessness services to more than 18,000 people each year in the Bay Area. “People don’t go into shelter and transitional housing and come out of it magically earning $55 an hour, right? That’s really what you have to earn to be able to afford the Bay Area.” Wan fears HUD’s new funding restrictions will lead to a dramatic increase in homelessness. “Absent that money, people can’t pay rent,” she said. “The concern was, is, continues to be, that it’ll push those people out of housing.” Vivian Wan is CEO of Abode Services, a nonprofit that provides housing and homelessness services to about 18,000 each year across the Bay Area. Bay Area communities at risk of losing millions in homelessness funding Across the Bay Area, San Francisco, Alameda, and Santa Clara counties collectively receive more than $160 million in HUD funding each year to combat homelessness. Local officials, however, tell the NBC Bay Area Investigative Unit that between 40 and 65 percent of their funding could be cut because of the new restrictions on permanent housing programs. “Alameda County Health continues to be deeply concerned by HUD’s shift away from what we know works (i.e., permanent housing with individualized services to help people heal and stay housed),” Troy Espera, communications director for Alameda County Health, wrote in a statement. “This poses a challenge and local jurisdictions are struggling with the whiplash between HUD and legal actions.” Nationally, at least 97,000 people living in federally funded permanent housing could be at risk of losing their housing under the new rules, according to the National Alliance to End Homelessness, an advocacy group that joined Santa Clara County and eight other local governments and nonprofits in filing litigation against HUD to challenge the federal government’s new funding restrictions. Nonprofits, local governments sue HUD to halt its new funding rules Last month, those plaintiffs won a partial victory when a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to throw out its application process. The court found HUD failed to give the public required notice and an opportunity to comment on the changes before the new funding restrictions were implemented. Since the court determined HUD’s grant process was “procedurally invalid,” it declined to weigh in on the lawsuit’s other challenges, including the merits of HUD’s new funding restrictions. HUD later appealed and earlier this month a federal appeals court allowed HUD to restart the application process with the same funding changes while the court reviews the case. In granting the stay, the appeals court said HUD had made a “strong showing that it is likely to succeed” on the merits of its argument that the $1.3 billion in funding it set aside for transitional housing and other supportive services was not subject to that notice-and-comment requirement. The appeals court also determined further delays could create funding gaps for homelessness programs across the country. Opponents, including Santa Clara County, are still challenging HUD’s new policies in court, but the clock is ticking. Applications are now due to HUD by Wednesday at 5 p.m. PT. Congress requires HUD to award the funds by December 1. “I think there’s no doubt that there is a risk that the funding will not be issued when it’s supposed to be issued,” LoPresti said. “I think everybody’s concerned about that right now.” Contact The Investigative Unit submit tips | 1-888-996-TIPS | e-mail Bigad Follow @BigadShaban on social media Bigad Shaban

headlines.title: 2 rescued after being swept into ocean at Panther Beach in Santa Cruz County
headlines.description: A man and woman were rescued from the ocean at Panther Beach in Santa Cruz County Tuesday afternoon. The couple was fishing on the rocks when they were swept into the water, according to Cal Fire. The circumstances leading up to the incident were not immediately clear. Rescue swimmers from the Santa Cruz Fire Department and California State Parks Public Safety pulled them from the water and provided medical aid. A Cal Fire helicopter then hoisted them up the steep cliff before they were taken to a hospital.

headlines.title: Watch: 1-on-1 interview with California governor candidate Steve Hilton
headlines.description: California will choose a new governor in November to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. Voters will decide between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years and also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. He recently joined NBC Bay Area for a wide-ranging discussion about his gubernatorial campaign, political philosophy and policy proposals. Watch the full one-on-one interview with Raj Mathai in the video above. Elections Sep 17 Elections Sep 14 Decision 2026 Jun 5 Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. NBC Bay Area reached out to Becerra multiple times for an interview and his campaign denied the requests. Since winning the primary, Becerra has kept a relatively low profile and has held a handful of public events, including an appearance in September at a rally in support of Proposition 1. Becerra did sit down for an interview with NBC Bay Area’s sister station, NBC Los Angeles, back in April. Watch the interview below.

headlines.title: San Francisco pub owner charged with assault
headlines.description: A well-known owner of three pubs in San Francisco has been charged with robbery and assault with a deadly weapon. Cyril Hacket, owner of Mad Dog in the Fog, Kezar Pub and Murio’s Trophy Room, is accused of walking into a shop called Further in the Haight Ashbury neighborhood with a bat. A security video from Saturday showed Hacket swinging the bat and walking out with a jacket from the shop’s rack. Witnesses said the confrontation followed a parking dispute that happened earlier in the day. District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said the investigation is still ongoing. She’s asking anyone with information to call San Francisco police.

headlines.title: Missing swimmer out of Antioch found dead
headlines.description: A swimmer who went missing last week in Antioch was discovered deceased, police said Tuesday. Edgielyn Torrente, 46, went missing while swimming near Smith’s Landing Seafood Grill on Wednesday. Torrente was found deceased in the San Joaquin River on Sunday. Just after 7 a.m. Sunday, officers responded to calls reporting a person in the water west of Smith’s Landing. The Contra Costa County Sheriff’s Office Marine Patrol and the Pittsburg Police Department recovered Torrente about a mile west of where she went missing. The Sheriff’s Office Coroner’s Division will determine the cause and manner of death. No foul play is suspected, according to police.

headlines.title: Pedestrian struck, killed by vehicle in SF's Richmond District
headlines.description: A pedestrian died after being struck by a motorist in San Francisco’s Richmond District on Monday afternoon, according to police. The collision was reported at 2:08 p.m. at the intersection of Arguello Boulevard and Anza Street. The pedestrian was taken to a hospital but died there, San Francisco police said. The driver of the vehicle involved in the collision stayed at the scene and cooperated with investigators, according to police. The name of the pedestrian was not immediately available.

headlines.title: OpenAI developer conference draws protests as company unveils new AI agents
headlines.description: Amid growing fears about the power of artificial intelligence and surrounded by protesters, OpenAI held its annual developer conference on Tuesday. The maker of ChatGPT also introduced new products during the event. Business and tech reporter Scott Budman reported that the focus of the day — and the reaction to it —depended on where you were standing. Inside the venue, the emphasis was on utilizing ChatGPT and other AI offerings rolled out by the company to make life easier. Outside, it was about demanding answers regarding safety concerns and fears that the city is turning into an AI-only enclave. As OpenAI CEO Sam Altman took the stage to cheers, a crowd outside San Francisco’s Fort Mason chanted his name in protest, shouting, “Sam Altman, get off it; choose people over profit.” Artificial intelligence Sep 26 Artificial intelligence Sep 22 Artificial intelligence Sep 17 Inside, the company showcased the latest version of its AI agents, called “Dots”. “This is the real-deal version of AI that we’ve always imagined for ourselves. It’s like an AI that always has your back, inspired by movies we all watched growing up,” presenters shared. The new agents can answer questions and execute tasks for users, acting as “a second set of eyes across everything I give it access to, and more importantly, a second set of hands to actually take work off my plate.” Outside, demonstrators focused on economic inequality and broader anxieties about what AI could do to humanity rather than for humanity. Many argued that the technology’s dominance in San Francisco is forcing long-term residents out. “We know that as soon as these IPOs happen, as soon as more money comes flowing into the city, we’re going to see a lot more evictions, and we need to be ready to scale up this fight,” said Molly Goldberg of the SF Anti-Displacement Coalition. It is a conflict over both money and safety tied to what all sides believe could be transformational technology.

headlines.title: 2 killed, 3 injured in multi-vehicle crash in East Palo Alto
headlines.description: Two people were killed and at least three others were injured in a seven-vehicle crash in East Palo Alto Tuesday morning, according to the San Mateo County Sheriff’s Office. The crash happened at about 8:20 a.m. in the area of Bay Road and University Avenue. Investigators said a minivan struck six other vehicles, including a SamTrans Ride Plus van, before coming to rest on Bay Road. The driver of the minivan, an adult man, suffered serious injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene. An adult woman who was also in the minivan was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries, where she later died. At least three other people were injured in the crash. None of those injuries were reported as life-threatening, according to the sheriff’s office. The cause of the crash is under investigation. Anyone who witnessed the crash or has additional information is asked to contact the San Mateo County Sheriff’s Office at 650-363-4911.
